To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Fake pills - please read this properly and talk to your kids this week

I'm writing this as a mum from round here, and I'll be upfront that I work in intensive care. I'm not going to say anything about anyone I've looked after, so don't ask - that's not what this is. This is about the police warning posted on here last week, which most people have scrolled straight past, and about the thread about Saturday that's turned into rumours and people having a go at kids.

I get why. It's frightening. But being frightened quietly, or being angry out loud, isn't going to keep anybody safe this weekend.

The tablets are blue and they're being sold as diazepam or Xanax. Some of them contain nitazenes - synthetic opioids that can be far stronger than heroin. You cannot tell by looking. Same colour, same shape, same marking as the ones that are just diazepam. Kids are buying them thinking they're getting something mild and getting something that stops their breathing.

The signs are extreme drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, slow or noisy breathing and blue lips. If someone's going floppy and you can't properly wake them, or their breathing has gone slow or noisy, or their lips are going blue, that is an emergency. Ring 999 straight away. Not in twenty minutes once you've seen how they are. Not after you've rung round their mates to find out what they took.

And please, do not put them to bed to sleep it off. I know that's what people do - it feels like the kind thing, letting them sleep it off, keeping them out of trouble. It's the worst thing you can do. By the time someone checks on them hours later, the brain has been without oxygen far too long, and that's not something anyone can undo. The window where someone can be brought back is short. Minutes, not hours.

Nobody is going to get in trouble for ringing for an ambulance. The police have said themselves, in their own warning, that their priority is preserving life. That's their words. So if you're a teenager reading this and your mate goes down at a party, you ring 999. You don't worry about the police, or your parents, or getting your mate into bother. You ring, and you tell them exactly what you think they've taken. That's what saves people.

There's also naloxone - a nasal spray that reverses an opioid overdose. Brightpath, the drug and alcohol service on Stockport Road next to the launderette, gives kits out free. Anyone can ask. No names, no referral, no lecture. Ten minutes' training and you walk out with a kit. Open Monday to Friday, 10 till 4, and Thursdays till 7. If you've got a teenager, or you are one, go and get one and learn how to use it. It might be your friend.

Parents - talk to your kids this week. Not after half term, not when it's all calmed down. This week. Over tea, no big lecture. Ask what they've heard, what's going round school, whether anyone's offered them anything. I had this exact conversation with my own 14-year-old last night. Eye roll, obviously. Then he asked me what pinpoint pupils meant, and we ended up talking properly for ten minutes. They do listen. They just don't want to look like they are.

And one last thing. Slagging off the kids involved helps nobody. Scared kids don't ring for help - that's the whole problem. If a teenager thinks they'll be in trouble, or their mate will, they'll put someone to bed and hope for the best. If your first reaction is "what were they doing there" or "that's the parents' fault", keep it to yourself and help keep them alive instead.

Please share this, not just like it. Share it to your own page, stick it in the school group chat, send it to one other parent. It's no good sat on a noticeboard where nobody reads it.

Thanks for reading. Becky
